section.title: A Weaned Soul at Rest
section.sectionRationale: A Song of Ascents of David, twelfth in the pilgrim collection Psalms 120 to 134, placed in Book V of the Psalter, Psalms 107 to 150. Among the shortest psalms, it distills a lifetime of hard-won humility into three verses, moving from personal contentment to a call for the whole nation to hope in the LORD.
section.thesis: A humble heart that refuses proud ambition finds a stilled and quieted soul, like a weaned child content in its mother's arms, and calls all God's people to the same settled hope in the LORD, a childlike trust perfectly embodied in Christ's own humility.
section.frameNote: Two movements: a humble, quieted heart before the LORD, verses 1 to 2, and the call for Israel to hope in the LORD forever, verse 3.

verses.text: My heart is not proud, O LORD, my eyes are not haughty. I do not aspire to great things or matters too lofty for me.
Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul; like a {{gamul|weaned child}} with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.

units.label: Put your hope in the LORD

verses.text: O Israel, put your hope in the LORD, both now and forevermore.

gamul.gloss: Weaned; a young child who has moved past need for the breast yet still rests securely against the mother, a picture of settled, dependent trust rather than restless craving, verse 2.

basic.context: Attributed to David, this brief Song of Ascents distills a hard-won lesson in humility, refusing proud ambition and instead finding a stilled, quieted soul like a weaned child resting in its mother's arms, before calling all Israel to the same settled hope in the LORD.
basic.hermeneutics: It describes David's own tested humility before the LORD, and it prescribes as an abiding pattern refusing proud ambition, cultivating a quieted soul content with God's provision, and placing hope in the LORD both now and forever.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm's central image is gamul, a weaned child, no longer restless for the breast yet still resting securely against the mother, a picture of mature, settled trust rather than either infantile craving or independent self-sufficiency.
basic.typology: The weaned child's settled trust anticipates the childlike faith Jesus commends as the pattern for entering the kingdom, and David's refusal of proud ambition anticipates Christ's own perfect humility, who did not grasp at equality with God but emptied Himself.
basic.christ: Jesus, though truly great, did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, Philippians 2:6-8, the perfect fulfillment of this psalm's refusal of proud ambition, and He calls His people to receive the kingdom like children, Mark 10:15.
basic.god: The LORD is the one before whom pride and lofty ambition are laid down, and He is the secure, mothering presence in whom a soul finds rest, not because all its needs are still being met moment by moment, but because it has learned settled contentment in Him.
basic.crossReferences: Philippians 2:6-8 shows Christ's supreme humility, refusing to grasp at what was rightfully His. Mark 10:15 calls disciples to receive the kingdom of God like a little child. 1 Peter 5:6-7 calls believers to humble themselves and cast every anxiety on God, who cares for them.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's picture of a humble heart and a weaned, settled soul is fulfilled in Christ's own perfect humility, and it calls believers, like Him, to lay down proud ambition and rest in childlike, settled hope in the LORD forever.

context.literary:
Psalm 131 is one of the shortest psalms in the whole Psalter, and it is shaped with care. Verse 1 is three negatives: the heart is not proud, the eyes are not haughty, the feet do not walk in great things. Heart, eyes and walk gather up the whole person, inner life, outlook and conduct. Verse 2 then answers with an oath-like 'Surely,' and the three negatives are replaced by two positive verbs, 'stilled' and 'quieted,' and one picture, the child on its mother.

The simile is repeated, as in Psalm 130:6. 'Like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.' The first line places the child against the mother; the second brings the picture inside, so that the comparison becomes a statement about the singer's own soul. The preposition rendered 'with' means literally 'upon' or 'against,' which gives the picture a physical closeness, a child lying on the mother's lap or carried at her side.

The poem is also built on a turn from 'I' to 'Israel.' For two verses the speaker talks to the LORD about himself, and then in verse 3 he turns around and addresses the people with the same words that ended Psalm 130:7, 'O Israel, put your hope in the LORD.' The pairing of the two psalms is deliberate. Psalm 130 ended its hope with a vast redemption still to come; Psalm 131 shows what a soul looks like that has learned to wait for it. The final phrase, 'both now and forevermore,' stretches the quiet of verse 2 over all time.
context.historical:
The title ties the psalm to David, and the setting that suits it best is his own story. He was anointed as a boy, Samuel's word made him a future king, and yet for years he waited while Saul hunted him. Twice he held Saul's life in his hands and refused to take it, saying he would not 'stretch out my hand against the LORD's anointed,' 1 Samuel 26:9-11, and he was stricken when he even cut a corner of Saul's robe, 1 Samuel 24:4-7. A man who could say 'I do not aspire to great things' was a man who had practised not grabbing a throne that was promised to him.

Weaning was a real event in Israel. A child might nurse for several years, and the day he was weaned was marked with a feast, as when Abraham 'held a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned,' Genesis 21:8. Hannah kept Samuel at home until he was weaned and then took him to Shiloh, 1 Samuel 1:22-24. A weaned child was no longer fretting at the breast, yet still depended on the mother for his place in the world. That is the human picture the psalm borrows.

Song of Ascents also means pilgrims. A crowd climbing to Jerusalem needed this lesson. The road was full of travellers, the city was the seat of kings and priests, and it was easy to feel small or to want a larger place. David's own contentment with a place at God's feet is held out as the way to approach the sanctuary. Placed next to Psalm 132, which is about his zeal for the ark, it also shows that the man who danced before the LORD and was despised for it, 2 Samuel 6:20-22, knew how to be small.
context.canonical:
The Bible is full of lowly people lifted by God and of proud people brought down, and Psalm 131 is the quiet voice of the first group. Proverbs 16:18 warns that 'Pride goes before destruction,' and Isaiah 2:11 says that 'the proud look of man will be humbled.' The psalm's refusal of lofty looks belongs to the same stream as Psalm 101:5, where the king will not endure 'the one with haughty eyes and a proud heart.' By contrast, Isaiah 66:2 says that God esteems 'he who is humble and contrite in spirit,' and Micah 6:8 asks for a walk that is humble with God.

The psalm's image of a settled child also has other voices around it. Psalm 22:9-10 remembers being 'secure at my mother's breast,' and Isaiah 66:12-13 describes God's comfort in nursing language, 'As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you.' Isaiah 49:15 goes further and says God will not forget His people even if a nursing mother could. The psalm, however, does not call God a mother; it describes the singer as a child.

In the New Testament Jesus takes up the child picture directly. 'Unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven,' Matthew 18:3, and 'anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it,' Mark 10:15. He thanks the Father that He has hidden things 'from the wise and learned' and revealed them 'to little children,' Matthew 11:25. Peter closes his own counsel with the psalm's logic: 'Humble yourselves, therefore, under God's mighty hand, so that in due time He may exalt you. Cast all your anxiety on Him,' 1 Peter 5:6-7. And Paul's hymn in Philippians 2:5-11 is the greatest statement of the same stance, because it is what the Son did.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wanted the singers to be able to say something that is rarely true: that they had settled the question of their own greatness. It is not a boast. The sentence begins with what the singer is not, and ends with a child. The point is that humility is not a performance of smallness. It is a rest. A proud person is always on his feet, measuring himself against others and reaching for more. A person who has stilled his soul has stopped reaching because he has found where he belongs.

The verb 'stilled and quieted' tells the first hearers that this quiet was achieved. The Hebrew has the sense of a deliberate act: 'Surely I have.' It was not the natural state of a restless heart but the result of putting something down. David is teaching pilgrims that peace comes from deciding that some things, 'matters too lofty for me,' are God's business and not theirs.

The call to Israel at the end shows the aim. The psalm is meant to be sung together, so that a whole people on a road full of ambitions and anxieties would practise the same quiet, with their hope placed in the LORD and not in their own reach.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes David's own condition, and it does not command a person to feel serene. It would be a misreading to take it as a rule that no one may aim high, study hard, lead, build or pursue a calling. David was a king, and Scripture praises diligence and wisdom. What the psalm refuses is a particular kind of reaching: pride that exalts the self, and a curiosity that tries to stand where only God can stand.

The pattern it commends is clear and carries over: bring ambition, anxiety and the questions we cannot answer into the presence of God, and rest in what He has shown. In practice that can mean doing the work in front of us without demanding to see how God will arrange everything, which is also what Jesus teaches in Matthew 6:25-34. A person under real pressure may not feel the calm of verse 2. The psalm still sets the direction: that calm is to be sought by trust, not produced by pretending.

debates.question: Does 'matters too lofty for me' forbid ambition altogether, or only a proud overreaching?

views.label: A general call to contentment
views.case: The mood of the whole psalm is modesty, and the verse reads as a rule of life: be content with the place God has given and do not strive for more. Paul's counsel in Romans 12:16, 'Do not be proud, but enjoy the company of the lowly,' fits that reading.

views.label: A refusal of proud, self-exalting overreach
views.case: David was himself called to great things, and it would be odd for him to disown all large responsibility. On this view the verse rejects arrogant reaching beyond one's calling, or the arrogance of wanting to understand God's hidden purposes, as in Job 42:3, 'things too wonderful for me to know.'

debates.bearing: On either reading the test is the source of the aim. Ambition that comes from a call and is carried out in dependence on God is not the pride the psalm renounces; ambition that is driven by the need to be someone else is.

debates.question: Is the child a weaned child or a nursing baby, and why does it matter?

views.label: The weaned child, secure but no longer craving
views.case: The Hebrew word names a child who has been weaned. That child no longer cries for milk, but still rests against the mother. Isaiah 28:9 uses 'infants just weaned' for the very young, so the child in view is small and still wholly dependent, and the picture is of contentment without demands.

views.label: A general picture of a baby at rest
views.case: Some read the image more loosely, as a symbol of trusting dependence, and note that Psalm 22:9 uses the nursing infant for security. On this view the exact stage of the child is less important than the quiet in the arms.

debates.bearing: The stage matters. A nursing infant trusts because the mother gives; a weaned child trusts the mother herself. The psalm describes faith that has moved from wanting what God gives to being satisfied with God.

debates.question: Does the mother in the simile tell us something about God?

views.label: A human picture only
views.case: The psalm says the singer's soul is like a weaned child with his mother. It never says God is a mother. The mother is part of the simile, and the LORD is addressed in the second person in verse 1 and as the object of hope in verse 3.

views.label: A hint of God's maternal tenderness
views.case: Other Scriptures do use nursing and comfort language of God, Isaiah 66:13 and Isaiah 49:15, and Jesus likens Himself to a hen gathering her chicks. A reader may fairly hear in the psalm the same tenderness.

debates.bearing: The psalm itself rests on the simile, and the safest course is to hear the tenderness without making the verse a statement about God's nature. Other texts give that doctrine more directly.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm's vocabulary is simple, and each choice is worth noticing. The first word is the verb for 'proud,' from the root gavah, to be high or lifted up. The verse pairs it with another verb meaning to be raised, in the line about the eyes. Together they paint the lifted head and the high look of arrogance, which Proverbs 6:16-17 names among the things the LORD hates. The singer's heart has not climbed up and his eyes have not looked down on others.

The third line says literally, 'I do not walk in great things and in things too wonderful for me.' The verb is the ordinary one for walking, which suggests a way of life and not a single desire. The second noun comes from the family of pele, 'wonder,' used for God's marvellous works. In Psalm 139:6 the same idea appears as knowledge that is 'too wonderful for me,' and in Job 42:3 as 'things too wonderful for me to know.' This word more often points to God's own works, which hints that the singer is declining to enter the territory that belongs to God.

Verse 2 begins with a Hebrew formula, 'if I have not,' which in biblical speech works as a self-curse and is rendered 'Surely.' The singer swears to the truth of his statement. The two verbs that follow are 'stilled' and 'quieted.' The first comes from a root meaning to level or make even, a smoothing of rough ground. The second is from damam, to be silent, the same root behind the command 'Be still before the LORD' in Psalm 37:7 and the 'rest' of Psalm 62:5. The soul that was heaving has been made flat and silent.

Then comes the picture, gamul, 'weaned.' It is the passive participle of the verb gamal, which is the verb used of weaning in Genesis 21:8 and 1 Samuel 1:22-24. This verb is also used elsewhere for dealing with someone in a way they deserve, but here it simply describes a child brought through the transition from milk to food. The child is described as gamul 'upon' its mother. In the second line the same preposition is used of the soul, 'upon me my soul,' as if the soul lay quieted on the singer himself and he was mother and child at once.

The last verse repeats the opening of Psalm 130:7, 'put your hope,' with the verb yachal. The word is used of waiting for God with expectation, as in Psalm 119:114, and it joins the two psalms. The phrase 'both now and forevermore' translates 'me'attah ve'ad olam,' a frequent closing in the Psalter, which makes the quiet of the psalm a quiet without end.

typology.type: The weaned child on its mother, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: Jesus set a child in the middle of His disciples and said that whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest in the kingdom, Matthew 18:2-4, and that the kingdom must be received like a child, Mark 10:15. The psalm's picture is about trust that does not demand. The New Testament escalates it by naming the Father to whom the child belongs, and by making childlikeness a condition of entering. The type falls short in that David's quiet was learned, while the child Christ speaks of is also one adopted into God's family, Romans 8:15.

David would not take the throne from Saul by force, and waited for the LORD to hand it over, 1 Samuel 26:9-11. Christ is the one who did not 'consider equality with God something to be grasped,' Philippians 2:6, and who refused the shortcut of the tempter, who offered the kingdoms of the world without the cross. The correspondence is real, since both receive a kingdom by waiting. The escalation is in the cost: David waited through exile, Christ through death on a cross, and God 'exalted Him to the highest place,' Philippians 2:9.

typology.type: The lowly lifted, verse 3 in the light of Luke 1:52
typology.fulfillment: Mary's song says God 'has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble,' Luke 1:52. The psalm's quiet hope that God will do right by the small is answered in the birth of Jesus in lowliness, and in the way He lived among the weary, Matthew 11:28-30, and washed feet, John 13:3-5. The pattern is that God's exaltation follows humility; it falls short only in that it applies to Jesus uniquely, because He alone was humble without sin.

study.christ:
Psalm 131 leads to Christ most plainly as a portrait of the mind He showed. Paul asks the Philippians to 'do nothing out of selfish ambition or empty pride, but in humility consider others more important than yourselves,' and then gives the pattern: Christ, 'existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,' Philippians 2:3-8. The psalm's refusal to reach for matters too lofty finds its deepest fulfilment in One who could rightly have reached for the highest place and chose to descend. The exaltation follows. 'Therefore God exalted Him to the highest place,' Philippians 2:9. This is exactly the order the psalm's world expects, with humility first, and God's lifting after.

He also embodies the stilled soul. He slept in a boat in a storm, and He told the weary, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest,' describing Himself as 'gentle and humble in heart,' Matthew 11:28-29. Those words, 'rest for your souls,' echo the psalm's picture of a soul at peace. The One who invites others to rest is the One who first lived in that rest toward the Father. Even in Gethsemane, when His soul was troubled, He placed Himself in His Father's hands.

He is the teacher of the child's way. Jesus rejoiced in the Spirit that the Father had hidden things from the wise and revealed them to little children, Luke 10:21. He called a child into the middle of an argument about who was greatest, Mark 9:33-37, and told His followers they must receive the kingdom like a little child, Luke 18:17. And on the night before His death, knowing the Father 'had delivered all things into His hands,' He wrapped a towel around His waist and washed the disciples' feet, John 13:3-5. A man who held everything could be small, because He was secure.

Finally, He is the one for whom the psalm's closing call is fulfilled. 'O Israel, put your hope in the LORD, both now and forevermore.' The hope of Israel stood in One who would come, and in Him that hope has a name, and the forevermore is secured by a resurrection, Romans 1:3-4.

A word of care. The psalm is David's, not Christ's, and it includes no language that only a sinless man could speak. We should not make the singer into Jesus. The psalm shows a human pattern of humility that Christ perfected, and it prepares the ear for the gospel's call to humble ourselves, 1 Peter 5:6-7.
study.god:
The God of Psalm 131 is the one before whom a person can stop striving. That is not a small claim. In a world where every person has to prove something, the psalm presents a God who is large enough to be trusted with the things we cannot control. The things 'too lofty' are not hidden because He is cruel, but because He is God and we are not. Romans 11:33-34 exclaims over the same fact, 'How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!', and ends in praise, not frustration.

He is also a God who cares about the posture of the heart. The psalm's three negatives, heart, eyes and walk, suggest that He looks at the inner person. James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5 quote Proverbs for the principle that 'God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.' This is not an arbitrary preference. A proud heart is one that has taken the place of God, so the opposition is also mercy, since a person who has taken God's seat cannot rest.

He is a God who lifts those who are low. Isaiah 57:15 says that He who is 'high and lifted up' dwells 'with the oppressed and humble in spirit.' It is one of the Bible's wonders that the highest God is found among the lowest. Hannah's song, Mary's song and Paul's reflection in 1 Corinthians 1:27-29 all say the same, that God chooses what the world despises, 'so that no one may boast in His presence.'

He is, at the same time, a God of tender care. The psalm borrows the picture of the child and its mother, and elsewhere God compares His comfort to a mother's, Isaiah 66:13, and promises not to forget His people, Isaiah 49:15. It matters that the quiet in the psalm is not isolation. The child lies on its mother. Peace is relational. 'Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you,' 1 Peter 5:7.

He is faithful across time. The final line sets hope in the LORD 'both now and forevermore,' and that is only reasonable if the LORD is the same today and tomorrow. A person can settle in the present only because the future is also held.

For worship, the psalm teaches a particular kind of prayer: not asking for more, but stopping. It invites us to lay down the need to understand and to win, and to be with God the way a child is with a mother, simply there, and content to be.

crossReferences.note: Paul sets selfish ambition and empty pride against the humility of Christ, who did not grasp at equality with God but emptied Himself. It is the psalm's refusal of lofty things lived out by the Son, and it supplies the reason a believer can lay down self-promotion.

Jesus is indignant that the children are kept away from Him and says the kingdom of God must be received like a little child. He then takes them in His arms. The psalm's weaned child on its mother is the posture He asks of every disciple.

Jesus thanks the Father for revealing things to little children and then invites the weary to find rest for their souls in Him, since He is gentle and humble in heart. The words about rest echo verse 2 and show who gives the rest.

Peter quotes 'God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble' and then tells believers to humble themselves under God's mighty hand and cast all their anxiety on Him. It is the psalm turned into instruction, with the added assurance that He cares.
'Rest in God alone, O my soul, for my hope comes from Him.' It uses a word for silence related to the psalm's 'quieted,' and ties the quiet soul to hope in the same way verse 3 does.

The LORD promises peace like a river and says, 'As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you.' It shows the image of a nursed child used of God's care for His people, which gives the psalm's picture a wider setting.

'Such knowledge is too wonderful for me, too lofty for me to attain.' A close parallel to verse 1 in its language, but with a different tone: here the limit of knowledge leads to wonder and trust, not frustration.

After the whirlwind, Job admits he spoke of 'things too wonderful for me to know.' It is the other side of the psalm: a man who learns by hard experience what David had learned to say in advance, that some things belong to God alone.

The disciples ask who is greatest in the kingdom, and Jesus sets a child before them. 'Whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greatest.' The quiet child of Psalm 131 is the answer to their question.

David will not lift his hand against the LORD's anointed, even though he has the chance and his men urge him. It shows the singer of verse 1 in action, a man who left the timing of his own greatness in God's hands.

Another Song of Ascents about eyes. Here the eyes look to the LORD like servants to a master's hand, 'until He shows us mercy,' under the contempt of the proud. It sets the psalm's humble eyes beside a people who suffer the pride of others.

study.oneStory:
The first sin in the Bible was a reach. The woman saw that the fruit was desirable, and the serpent promised that she would be 'like God,' and a whole world fell for the sake of a position that was not hers. Ever since, human history has been the record of people trying to be bigger than they are, and of the consequences, from Babel's tower to the empires of the prophets. Psalm 131 is a small, quiet, deliberate step back from that story. It shows a man who has put down the reach.

It is a rare moment in the Old Testament, because it shows what a restored human heart looks like before the work of Christ is done. David's life was no model of perfection, and the Bible does not hide his falls. But here he gives voice to what God's people are meant to become: people whose sense of themselves does not depend on how high they have risen. The psalm trains Israel for a coming king who would be unlike the kings of the nations, one who would be 'gentle and humble in heart,' Matthew 11:29.

Then the story reaches its centre. The Son, who had every right to the highest place, did not grasp it, but went down to a cross, Philippians 2:6-8, and so reversed Adam's reach. He did what Adam would not do, trusted His Father, and the Father exalted Him, Philippians 2:9-11. Everyone who is joined to Him is taught the same stance, and promised the same outcome: 'Humble yourselves, therefore, under God's mighty hand, so that in due time He may exalt you,' 1 Peter 5:6.

The church lives between the two stories. It is still tempted to reach, and still called back to the child's quiet. And the end of the story is the child's quiet made permanent. In the new creation there is no more striving to be someone, since every believer is known and loved by the Lamb, and rules with Him not by grasping but by receiving, Revelation 22:5. The psalm's last words, 'both now and forevermore,' are a promise about that.

sermon.title: That's Life!
sermon.why: Begg treats Psalms 129 to 131 together, showing how this psalm's picture of a humble, weaned soul completes the sequence's movement from affliction, through forgiveness, to settled contentment in the LORD.

quiz.q: What does David deny about his own heart and eyes in verse 1?

options.text: That his heart is proud or his eyes haughty.
options.note: This is the exact denial that opens the psalm's confession of humility.

options.text: That he has any love for the LORD.
options.note: The psalm is a confession of humble devotion to the LORD, not a denial of love for Him.

options.text: That he has ever sinned in any way.
options.note: The psalm addresses pride and ambition specifically, not a blanket claim of sinlessness.

options.text: That he has any physical eyesight at all.
options.note: Haughty eyes is a figure of speech for arrogance, not a statement about literal eyesight.

quiz.q: What does David say he does not aspire to, according to verse 1?

options.text: Great things or matters too lofty for him.
options.note: This is the exact phrase describing the ambition David deliberately refuses.

options.text: Any form of daily work or responsibility.
options.note: The psalm addresses proud overreaching, not ordinary work or responsibility.

options.text: A relationship with the LORD.
options.note: The psalm is entirely about David's relationship with the LORD, not a rejection of it.

options.text: Basic provisions like food and shelter.
options.note: The 'lofty matters' in view are things beyond one's place or calling, not basic needs.

quiz.q: What image does verse 2 use to describe David's stilled soul?

options.text: A weaned child resting with its mother.
options.note: This is the exact image the psalm uses for a settled, quieted soul.

options.text: A soldier resting after victorious battle.
options.note: The image is domestic and intimate, a weaned child with its mother, not a soldier's rest.

options.text: A ship anchored safely in a storm.
options.note: The specific image given is a weaned child, not a ship or anchor.

options.text: An eagle soaring high above the clouds.
options.note: The image is one of quiet closeness and rest, not soaring flight.

quiz.q: What does verse 3 call all Israel to do?

options.text: Put their hope in the LORD, both now and forevermore.
options.note: This is the psalm's exact closing exhortation to the whole nation.

options.text: Abandon hope during difficult seasons.
options.note: The verse calls for enduring hope, the opposite of abandoning it.

options.text: Place their hope only in future generations.
options.note: The hope commanded is in the LORD Himself, not merely in future descendants.

options.text: Hope in the LORD only during times of prosperity.
options.note: The phrase 'now and forevermore' calls for hope in every season, not only prosperous ones.

quiz.q: How does Christ fulfill this psalm's refusal of proud, lofty ambition?

options.text: Though equal with God, He did not grasp at that equality but emptied Himself in humility.
options.note: Philippians 2:6-8 shows Christ's supreme humility as the fulfillment of this psalm's refusal of pride.

options.text: He demanded recognition of His full glory from the very beginning of His ministry.
options.note: Philippians 2 describes Christ's self-emptying humility, the opposite of demanding recognition.

options.text: He rejected all forms of authority and rule.
options.note: Christ humbled Himself yet was also exalted and given all authority, not a rejection of rule as such.

options.text: He taught that ambition of any kind is always sinful.
options.note: The concern is proud, self-exalting ambition, not diligent service exercised in humility.

questions: David refuses to aspire to 'great things too lofty' for him. Where might restless ambition be robbing you of contentment in the place God has actually called you?
The image of a weaned child describes a soul no longer frantic but settled and at rest. Would you describe your own soul right now as restless or as quieted before God?
This settled trust was hard won, likely through David's own experiences of hardship and discipline. What season of difficulty has taught you deeper contentment in God rather than in circumstances?
The psalm calls all Israel, not just David, to hope in the LORD 'now and forevermore.' Is your hope in God tied mainly to present circumstances, or does it stretch into an enduring, forever hope?
Christ modeled the ultimate humility, refusing to grasp at what was rightfully His. Where do you need to follow His example and lay down pride or entitlement this week?

translationNotes.note: Haughty eyes is a common Hebrew idiom for arrogance, since a proud posture is often reflected first in the eyes and bearing, Proverbs 6:17.
In the ancient Near East, weaning often occurred around age three, making the image one of a child old enough to have moved past desperate need yet still choosing closeness and rest with its mother.
Now and forevermore mirrors the closing phrase of Psalm 125:2, tying this psalm's personal humility to the same enduring, communal hope in the LORD.
